body.text: Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72
The Lachie Neale case saw the AFL take a gut-feel approach to a gut punch
It was a gut-feel approach to a gut punch that has left AFL fans baffled by the circus surrounding it.
Brisbane Lions superstar Lachie Neale is indeed free to play in the grand final tomorrow after successfully arguing that his impeccable character was enough to forego tribunal precedent.
But by the end of the whole drawn-out saga, the AFL's case against Neale was part Balogun, part popgun, and part Raygun in its absurdity and futility.

Part Balogun, in that fans could be forgiven for once again tasting that hint of bitterness in their mouths that accompanied FIFA's decision to allow US striker Folarin Balogun to play a knockout match despite being handed a red card in the previous game.
Part popgun, in that the AFL's approach all season of stamping out behind-the-ball gut punches with an instant one-week suspension ended with a whimper when it mattered most.

And part Raygun, in that they all flailed around indiscriminately in front of a captivated audience, who couldn't decide whether what they were watching was actually kind of brilliant in its blinding nonsense.
Nobody saw this coming, but everyone still somehow suspected it might arrive.

To compare it to the Balogun decision, where US President Donald Trump made a direct phone call to FIFA boss Gianni Infantino, is potentially unfair, yet the comparisons will come, and they already have.

This was not a sneaky phone call, or a threat, or a back-scratching exercise that so often permeates the world of sport, but a cartoonish widening of the eyes and a dimpling of the cheeks accompanied by an innocent, "Who, me?"

Using a precedent set earlier in the season when the AFL allowed Scott Pendlebury to escape with a fine for an offence that would usually attract a suspension via a "compelling and exceptional circumstances" provision, Neale's team argued that the 320-gamer was just as worthy as the Collingwood veteran for the same provision.

In Pendlebury's case, he was on the verge of becoming the most-capped AFL player in history, had never come close to a suspension, and was fronting the tribunal for an incident that happened in play and was deemed careless rather than deliberate.

In Neale's case, he had played 100 fewer games than Pendlebury, was fronting the tribunal for an incident that was clearly deliberate and behind the play, and, crucially, had been fined on three prior occasions for striking an opponent off the ball.

The decision to compare the two cases and conclude that Neale's case was on par with Pendlebury's will most baffle fans and open doors to veterans in future seasons to argue that their records need only compare to Neale's for them to all receive the "good bloke" discount when push comes to gut punch.

Meanwhile, the nine players who were suspended this year for similar actions to Neale's must question whether the AFL is as serious about body strikes as it says it is, or is only serious about it when the players don't have a couple of Brownlow Medals to their name and a grand final to play in on the weekend.
Make no mistake though, this is not a decision that comes with a bona fide outrage guarantee.
In an ABC Sport poll accompanying yesterday's live blog of the appeal, 42 per cent of the 47,000 respondents said they believed Neale should be free to play.

Footy legends from Matthew Richardson to Tony Shaw bemoaned the idea that a footballer could miss out on a grand final for a whack that in yesteryear would be considered a bit of a rib tickler, a gentle reminder to an opponent to stay out of your way and stop being a goose.
But 2026 is not yesteryear, and the AFL decided long ago that striking a player to the body behind play was not something that it would stand for.
Neale knew this, and did it anyway.

Yet he will lace up the boots and run out onto the MCG tomorrow after the AFL flipped and flopped, turned and tumbled, and kangaroo-bounced its way to a decision that has left at least half of the AFL world with its collective mouth agape, questioning whether what they just witnessed was real.

The Fremantle players standing across from Neale tomorrow will likely be torn as they attempt to win their club's first flag in 31 years of existence. On the one hand, not having Neale out there would have been a major leg up. On the other hand, they surely want to claim the premiership knowing they beat the Lions at their very best.
A Fremantle victory now becomes the most palatable result for the AFL.
Because if the Lions win a close one, and Neale goes on to star as he is wont to do, that victory will leave a sour taste in the mouths of those who believe the AFL should have stuck to its guns.
And for long-suffering Dockers fans, that prospect would be the greatest gut punch of all.
